stories.headline: Claude proved memory-safety properties at the RISC-V assembly level for 123 open-source libraries
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: after a month of AI finding bugs faster than anyone can patch them, this is the other half of the story, using models to prove code has no bugs of a given kind.
body: Anthropic and its collaborator Theorem report that Claude produced formal proofs, fully autonomously, that programs from 123 real open-source libraries always exit normally without memory-safety errors or failed assertions, for every input under 64 MB and every modeled Linux OS response and memory layout. The proofs are about compiled RISC-V binaries, under stated assumptions such as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget. The trick for getting a spec was turning each project's existing fuzz and test harnesses into the rule that the test suite always passes.

For scale, the post recalls that the seL4 kernel took two person-years to write and 20 person-years to verify. While writing these proofs Claude also turned up bugs that had survived years of testing. Anthropic is publishing a subset of the proofs plus its RISC-V and OS semantics, Theorem is offering to run the pipeline on other open-source projects and has a Claude skill to get started, and the post covers side experiments on zlib and on proving a Rust-written Python interpreter equivalent to the original. It is on the HN front page with more than 200 comments.

stories.headline: Three in four new Teslas in North America now ship with paid FSD, and Cybercab customer deliveries are targeted for December
stories.why_read: The software is now what people buy, and your Austin Robotaxi is apparently pricing above Uber and still filling up.
body: Per X News summaries of Tesla's Q3 materials, more than 75 percent of new North American deliveries in Q3 included paid FSD, up from 55 percent the quarter before. Active FSD users reached 1.74 million, with an average of about 2,800 paid subscribers added per day and roughly $92 million a month in revenue. Elon Musk's line was that people are now buying FSD with a car attached.

On the call, VP Lars Moravy said Tesla aims to hand the first steering-wheel-free Cybercabs to customers by December 2026, starting small; Musk said most Cybercabs will be Tesla-owned for ride service, with customer-owned cars joining the fleet by mid-2027 and Dallas next after Austin. James Cat's post, which you reposted, argues Austin Robotaxi demand and supply are settling at a price above Uber, meaning riders choose to pay more. Chuck Cook, also in your reposts, says FSD v15 brings a huge jump in parameter count, new capabilities for extra operating hours, high-speed roads and marginal weather, and new mapping and navigation that drops the third-party map dependency.

stories.headline: Quad9 will stop serving France on November 24 rather than block DNS answers for beIN
stories.why_read: The top story on HN, and a clean test case for whether a public resolver can stay neutral under copyright blocking orders.
body: Quad9, the Swiss nonprofit public DNS resolver, says a French court ruled in favor of beIN and ordered it to block recursive resolution of domains the broadcaster says infringe its sports rights. The court cut the penalty from €580,000 to €1,000 a day, but Quad9 says it cannot comply long term without altering DNS answers, which it calls a neutral, passive service it refuses to lie about.

So it is withdrawing its free service for users located in France as of Tuesday, November 24. Quad9 notes it has no connection to the domains or their operators and argues the courts misunderstood how DNS works. The HN thread, past 1,200 points, is debating whether resolvers should be treated like ISPs or like phone books.

stories.headline: eMudhra is leaving the public SSL/TLS certificate business after its CA incident
stories.why_read: You reposted the list of October incidents that included eMudhra. This is how that one ends.
body: eMudhra's board voted to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business. The chairman says the company revoked the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovery, that no end-entity certificates were issued from them, and that its infrastructure was not compromised. He says SSL/TLS is about 1 percent of revenue, rising compliance costs and free certificates have eroded the return, and the social media scrutiny was out of proportion to the business.

Its G1 RSA roots will keep serving customers through a transition worked out with browser root programs, affected customers will get free replacement certificates from partners, and revocation and status services will run until every issued certificate expires or is replaced. The HN thread, near 700 comments, is largely about how the browser root programs handled it.

stories.headline: Google Cloud's Agent Compute Engine gives every agent its own hardware-isolated microVM
stories.why_read: You reposted it. It's the hyperscaler version of the box your own bots run on, and the design notes are worth a systems person's time.
body: Richard Seroter announced Agent Compute Engine, a coming Google Cloud service that gives each AI agent its own hardware-isolated microVM with container-like speed and no credentials held inside the sandbox. Google says it already uses it internally. The engineering deep dive by distinguished engineers Ramanathan Venkatapathy and Rohit Jnagal frames it as the next shift after Borg containers, TPUs and the Titanium offload chips.

The motivating case was the Gemini goal of a personal cloud agent for every user, each needing a real computer with a filesystem, runtimes, a browser and network access. They split agents into a harness (the brain that calls the model) and a sandbox (the hands), and argue VMs are too slow to start and pause, containers don't isolate enough for coding agents that need root, and always-on VMs waste resources while agents wait between model steps. Target workloads include consumer agent surfaces, long-lived coding workspaces, large-scale RL and evals, and sandbox backends for Google services.

stories.headline: NVIDIA's OpenShell: a policy-enforced runtime for fleets of autonomous agents
stories.why_read: Same problem as Google's microVMs, but open source and something you could run yourself today.
body: OpenShell describes itself as a safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. The idea is that agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs and use credentials, so OpenShell lets you declare in a policy what each agent may touch and then enforces that, including instrumenting at the kernel level, instead of handing agents unrestricted access to data, secrets or the network.

The repository has about 1,850 commits and just moved to a 0.1.x line with a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, a larger extension surface and new APIs, with an upgrade guide. It is mostly Rust with Python SDK pieces and ships as a snap and via an install script. It reached the HN front page with more than 400 points.

stories.headline: SpaceXSI launches Grok for Startups and a 130-company Super Intelligence Partner Network
stories.why_read: It's the commercial push behind the Grok Bot and Grok Build tools you use daily.
body: Per X News, SpaceXSI rolled out Grok for Startups on October 22: a shared credit balance across Grok, Grok Build, Grok Bot and the Grok API, sized for six to twelve months of real use, with 20 percent available right away and dollar-for-dollar matching for up to six months. Early users cited automating sales follow-ups, recruiting and reports, and turning feature requests into code with cloud agents.

Alongside it, the SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network launched with more than 130 companies including NVIDIA, Bain & Company and Databricks, plus a deal with Tech Mahindra to modernize software in banking, healthcare and other regulated industries. It follows the Q3 report in which the Super Intelligence segment brought in $7.56 billion.

stories.headline: AI scanning has pushed new vulnerability reports past 10,000 a month, and the PHP embargo story shows the strain
stories.why_read: It ties together your October security reposts: disclosure processes built for human-speed bug finding are buckling.
body: Per X News, newly reported vulnerabilities have climbed from 1,000 to 2,000 a month in prior years to more than 10,000 recently as AI systems scan legacy codebases at scale, with CVE counts roughly doubling year over year while exploited flaws grow more slowly. Researchers like Omar Khattab say they still haven't seen superhuman feats in the most prized areas, and many point out that good results depend on the person prompting and iterating.

On HN, petecooper posted an apology for breaking the embargo on this week's PHP RCEs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, saying his contacts had told him there was no embargo and he only meant to warn others who compile PHP from source. Commenters were kind, and one pointed to an AWS threat intelligence post saying the bugs were already leaked and being exploited before his post.

stories.headline: Run a few agents whose only job is deleting tech debt
stories.why_read: You reposted it, and it's a practical pattern to try on your own repos this week.
body: Arpit Bhayani's tip: agents write code fast, so they also produce clutter fast, including dead code, near-duplicate helpers, unused imports, stale feature flags and comments that no longer match. Cleanup is work people rarely prioritize, so give it to dedicated cleanup agents.

His rules are to keep each agent narrow (one removes dead code, one merges duplicates, one fixes stale docs), keep each change to one small reviewable pull request, and let the test suite judge, since a cleanup is valid only if behavior is unchanged. A single make-it-better agent, he warns, will rewrite things it should leave alone. Deleting code is risky, but agents calling dead code because they think it's live is riskier.

stories.headline: What is a harness, and does it still matter? Developers argue it out
stories.why_read: You reposted Theo and the opencode AGENTS.md rule; this is the conversation they belong to.
body: X News sums up two days of debate: a harness is the layer that gives a model tools such as file edits and command execution, plus parsers and feedback loops, turning it into an agent. Theo explained it as the essential context-and-capabilities layer, Ramp described its in-house Laminar harness, and the trend is toward building your own for flexibility and observability. Skeptics say harness focus signals doubt in model progress; others cite tests where the same model costs and performs very differently, including 50 percent token savings.

One concrete harness rule you reposted via Dave Kiss, from opencode's AGENTS.md: before adding complexity for a speculative or very unlikely race or security edge case, explain the concrete failure mode, likelihood and complexity cost to the user and get their buy-in, and do not silently expand scope for theoretical robustness.

stories.headline: Verification is the bottleneck for coding agents, so Warp gives each one a computer and a highlight reel
stories.why_read: Two reposts from Warp engineers on a problem you hit with every bot you run: proving the agent's work actually works.
body: Varoon Kodithala, citing Addy Osmani's view that verification is the biggest bottleneck for coding agents, says Warp built a computer-use tool for Warp Factories: every agent gets a computer to navigate the apps it built, take screenshots and recordings, and post them for human review. Three to four minutes of activity get edited down to about 15 stitched clips with cursor clicks and key presses, which he says has sharply cut time to merge.

Sathvik's companion post argues software factories should be configured as code: in Warp, the factory lives in a repo as markdown and YAML, so agents, automations, runners, benchmarks and custom model routers sit in one place and can be improved like any other code. Ryan Snodgrass, also in your reposts, describes the CI side: checks under two minutes in the PR, longer tests in the merge queue, and the deepest tests after merge to main.

stories.headline: Skills over MCP can be personalized per user, and pstack shows what a skills methodology looks like
stories.why_read: Your bot fleet runs on skills; both posts you reposted are about where that layer is heading.
body: Pamela Fox highlighted a point from David Soria Parra: when an authenticated MCP server ships skills, it can send down skills specific to the logged-in user, maybe even personalized to them, a benefit of skills-over-MCP she hadn't considered.

Chen Cheng's long notes on poteto's pstack, which you also reposted, read it as a methodology rather than 56 separate skills: first build a verification skill and feature map so agents can run and drive the app themselves, then route work through fixed flows, and only then add parallelism and auto-merge. He highlights making apps drivable via JSON-output CLIs with dry-run flags, preferring switchable prototypes over adversarial review of abstract plans, and a four-level order for fixing repeated mistakes: architecture first, then lint or tests, then skills or rules, with human review last.

stories.headline: OpenAI on forward deployed engineering: the job is making yourself obsolete every few months
stories.why_read: You reposted it. It's useful framing for anyone doing customer-facing AI engineering inside a large company.
body: Tanay Jaipuria shared an OpenAI essay on what forward deployed engineering means there, summarizing it as a role that now involves making yourself obsolete every few months as the models absorb the work you were doing for customers.

The piece is on OpenAI's site. It lands in the same week OpenAI made its Decisions API generally available and expanded enterprise distribution through Google Cloud, so the FDE team is the human layer in that go-to-market.

stories.headline: AI infrastructure stocks have been crushed for a month, and Jensen Huang says neocloud funding will sort itself out
stories.why_read: You reposted the damage list; here's the bull case being made at the same time.
body: Shay Boloor's tally of the past month: Cipher down 57 percent, IREN down 48, Aehr down 47, Hut 8 down 39, CoreWeave down 38, Nebius down 36, Credo down 36, Arm down 36, Astera Labs down 33, Penguin down 32, TeraWulf down 32, Amkor down 31 and Intel down 31.

Per X News, Nvidia's Jensen Huang told investors that customer demand for neoclouds like Nebius will solve their capital shortages, and dismissed fears of a memory chip glut by 2029. Nebius just secured a $3.5 billion credit facility from Citi, backed by more than $40 billion in contracts from Microsoft and Meta.

stories.headline: Most AI token spending traces back to venture money, per Apollo and Ramp data
stories.why_read: It's the sharpest number yet on who is actually paying for inference, and why a funding slowdown would hit the labs.
body: Per X News, Apollo and Ramp data show the top 1 percent of AI token spenders, who make up most of the volume, are 80.4 percent VC-backed versus a 13.1 percent median, with Anthropic and OpenAI leading among US businesses. Chamath Palihapitiya estimates 70 to 75 cents of every token dollar traces back to venture funds.

Separately, the IMF warned of high valuations and about $1.4 trillion in circular financing, projecting a possible 1.1 percent drop in global GDP by 2028 if AI investment crashes, while many on X argue the constant warnings are themselves a sign there's no bubble.

stories.headline: Dwarkesh Patel's semiconductor manufacturing flashcards
stories.why_read: You reposted it. An easy way to retain the fab details from his Intel episode.
body: Dwarkesh Patel and his semiconductor tutor Will Michaels made a set of flashcards on chip manufacturing to go with the new Intel episode of his podcast, plus a further-reading list at the bottom of the page.
The site also has flashcard sets for his other technical episodes, including the one with Reiner Pope on LLM inference and Eric Jang on building AlphaGo from scratch.

stories.headline: Awesome Self-Hosted: a map for replacing SaaS with software you run yourself
stories.why_read: You reposted it, and it's the kind of list worth bookmarking for home lab weekends.
body: Bilgin Ibryam pointed to awesome-selfhosted, a curated list of free software network services and web apps you can host on your own servers, spanning communication, media, storage, developer tools, analytics, automation and much more.
The GitHub repo has about 329,500 stars and 7,100 commits, with a browsable version at awesome-selfhosted.net and a separate list for non-free software.

stories.headline: MiniMax opens the weights of M3.1 Flash, a 1M-context multimodal MoE
stories.why_read: A new open-weight model aimed at fast, cheap serving, with NVIDIA integrations day one.
body: Per X News, MiniMax released open weights for M3.1 Flash, a mixture-of-experts model that handles text, images and video with a 1-million-token context window. It reports 76.2 on BankerToolBench and 82.2 on CyberGym, runs three times faster than M3 at a third of the cost, and is priced at $0.15 per million input tokens via API.
Early community tests show it building interactive 3D scenes from single prompts, and integrations from NVIDIA and others enable serving above 1,000 tokens per second.

stories.headline: OXR, a 1.3B open model, tops three document-parsing benchmarks
stories.why_read: Small, fast and useful for RAG pipelines: PDFs with tables and formulas into clean Markdown or JSON.
body: Per X News, the SoMark team released OXR, a 1.3-billion-parameter open-source model that leads olmOCR-Bench (87.84), OmniDocBench (97.18) and DocParsingBench (87.76), processing about one page per second on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000. It recognizes 13 element types including tables, formulas, code blocks, chemical structures and handwriting, and outputs Markdown or JSON with bounding boxes.

It was trained with a recursive self-improvement loop instead of manual labeling. Code, weights and a demo are on GitHub and Hugging Face, and a companion release, OvisOCR3, adds compact multimodal features.

stories.headline: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017: an MIT-licensed model that runs locally and scores 78.1% on ARC-AGI-2
stories.why_read: Frontier-ish results on a 3090 or a Mac is exactly the open-model story you track.
body: Per X News, DeepSeek's mid-October open-weight release runs on everyday hardware like RTX 3090s and Macs at dozens to hundreds of tokens per second. Reported results include 78.1 percent on ARC-AGI-2 at $0.16 per task and rediscovering 87.5 percent of a set of cybersecurity CVEs at $2.40 each.
It is MIT-licensed and available on Hugging Face and hosts including NEAR AI Cloud, with claims that it matches top models on quality at far lower cost and about 12 times the speed.

stories.headline: OpenAI's Decisions API goes GA as one engineer dissects the Jev decision-model hype
stories.why_read: Decision models were all over your feed this week. Here's the product and the skeptic side by side.
body: Per X News, OpenAI made its Decisions API generally available. Powered by GPT-6 Luna, it answers quick questions about text, images or data with probabilities, choices or scores, handles up to 400 questions per request, and starts at $0.10 per million input tokens. OpenAI also moved OpenResponses to the Linux Foundation, and Uber expanded Codex and ChatGPT Work to 30,000 employees.

Alex Ewerlöf's essay on the Jev hype cycle, which hit the HN front page, argues Jev is basically a general-purpose classifier that needs little training data, that calling it a decision model is a stretch since it can't see or reason, and that the idea of non-autoregressive decision models goes back more than a year. He says Jev isn't dead but its hype is, while decision models as a category are rising.

stories.headline: Commerce offers up to $389M in CHIPS funding for power semiconductors for fusion and AI data centers
stories.why_read: Fusion and chips in one story, and Helion and Commonwealth Fusion are both on the list.
body: Per X News, the Commerce Department issued letters of intent for up to $389 million in CHIPS Act funding for advanced power semiconductors. Helion would get up to $175 million for high-voltage chips for its pulsed fusion systems in Washington and Vermont, alongside $50 million in private investment and more than 100 jobs. Commonwealth Fusion Systems would get up to $85 million for plasma heating and radiation-hardened components.

Vertical Semiconductor and Sibelco round it out with awards for AI-efficient power chips and high-purity quartz. The goal is to onshore critical components and ease fusion bottlenecks as data center electricity demand climbs.

stories.headline: A lost Schrödinger manuscript shows he backed indeterminism, and before quantum mechanics existed
stories.why_read: A short history-of-physics find that flips the usual story about Schrödinger and randomness.
body: ScienceAlert reports that physics historian Flavio Del Santo of the University of Geneva found a three-page Schrödinger manuscript that sat unpublished in an Austrian library for more than 80 years. It is a contribution to the long debate over whether the universe is fundamentally random or governed by hidden variables.

Rather than the discomfort with quantum randomness he is often portrayed as having, Schrödinger argued that some aspects of the universe cannot be predicted, a view he held even before quantum theory emerged in the 1920s. "The strongest plea in favor of indeterminism is older than quantum mechanics," he wrote.

stories.headline: Sampling the alien space of science: AI ideas no existing research community would think of
stories.why_read: A clever way to use AI for ideas that complement researchers instead of recombining what's already crowded.
body: A paper from Artiles, Schölkopf, Larochelle, Goyal, Rahaman and others argues that discovery is limited not just by what's true but by what's cognitively available to researchers, and that LLMs inherit that bias by recombining dense areas of the literature. Their method breaks papers into idea atoms, scores combinations for scientific coherence, and separately scores whether any existing author community is positioned to produce them, then picks coherent but unlikely combinations.

On 16,068 peer-reviewed LLM papers, the sampler produced more diverse research portfolios than frontier LLM baselines while matching or beating per-idea quality in blind evaluations. Using only pre-2025 data, picking under 1 percent of candidates recovered 2025 combinations at 35.9 times chance.

stories.headline: Dijkstra in 1978: On the foolishness of "natural language programming"
stories.why_read: Half the AI-coding debate on your timeline is relitigating this essay, so it's worth reading the original.
body: EWD 667 argues that the care and accuracy of formal symbolism is not an obstacle to programming but the point. Dijkstra recounts how high-level languages improved things by turning many silly mistakes into error messages instead of wrong answers, and questions the hope that machines instructed in our native tongues would make life easier.

His argument is that choosing an interface is not just dividing a fixed amount of labor between person and machine; natural language's ambiguity moves the burden rather than removing it. It resurfaced on the HN front page with more than 100 comments in the middle of this week's arguments about AI writing production code.

stories.headline: Docker is weird: notes from someone writing their own container runtime
stories.why_read: A friendly refresher on what containers really are, from your Unix and DevOps home turf.
body: The author is building a container runtime for fun and lists what surprised them: containers are just processes with restrictions you can find in /proc, made from several kernel features (namespaces, cgroups and networking pieces) rather than one container feature, and images are folders that get chroot or pivot_root applied.

The best section is on why Go is awkward for runc: Go's runtime is multi-threaded and has no real fork, so runc runs a C module before Go initializes to make single-threaded syscalls, and re-execs /proc/self/exe with a special argument to approximate fork. It also notes how easy it is to forget that the Docker daemon traditionally runs as root.

stories.headline: Ask HN: if the models are so good, why don't the labs just start 100 companies?
stories.why_read: A good thread on lab strategy that pairs with this week's VC token-spend data.
body: The question: if frontier models are so capable, why sell tokens as the main business instead of building companies that use them, especially as token prices fall?

Top answers: the labs are moving into the app layer and even consulting; during a gold rush you sell shovels, which is why they're investing in custom silicon; and selling tokens through long-running agents is the only thing provably growing revenue right now, at a time when capital is pricier than in the 2010s. The thread has nearly 200 comments.

stories.headline: Ask any frontier model for a controversial take on humans and you get the same one
stories.why_read: A fun, slightly unnerving experiment: twelve models, ten labs, one answer.
body: ModelCompare asked 12 models from ten labs in three countries for their most controversial take on humans, three times each, with no hedging. Every model gave the same take at least once, that people pick what their group believes and then invent reasons, and 7 of the 12 gave it every time.

Examples: GPT-6.1 Sol said humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth, Grok 4.7 said humans would rather be wrong together than right alone, and Gemini 4 Argon called consciousness a PR department. The irony that the models converged on a take about conformity is the HN thread's favorite point, at more than 450 comments.

stories.headline: How a frontier model hides secret messages in the SVG images it draws, and whether it can read them back
stories.why_read: A neat, concrete look at steganography by LLMs, which matters for agent monitoring.
body: Researchers on LessWrong asked Claude Fable 5.1, at maximum reasoning, to hide each of 50 short messages in an SVG image, then gave screenshots to a fresh Fable instance with no source code and no agreed scheme. Fable converged on a few styles that encode each letter as a visual element, and 33 of the 50 images used heights, such as a row of stars or buildings whose height marks a letter's place in the alphabet.

Many of the images were decoded by the second instance; the authors also briefly compare GPT-6 Astra on the same task. The open question for safety teams is how easily models could pass messages that humans skim right past.

stories.headline: Ashlee Vance on India's hard-tech wave, and why VCs should actually visit the factories
stories.why_read: You bookmarked his India story and reposted this follow-up, so here they are together.
body: Ashlee Vance says Sriram Rajagopalan and Lachy Groom have managed to fund a hard-tech revolution in India that most people have missed, and that he is very bullish on Indian commercial space: it will take a decade, but India is the only country with a real chance of competing alongside the US and China.

In the follow-up you reposted, he says he was surprised to learn VCs often don't fly out to see the hardware companies they invest in. Having walked through many factories, he says he can usually tell within five minutes what's real, and that his tour of Airbound in India showed touches of an early Rocket Lab in organization and attention to detail.
